title: 200 class-keyed rules vs 200 universal/attribute-keyed rules
variable: class-subject selectors vs universal + attribute selectors
claim: Antipattern #24 from web-performance-antipatterns-50.md: 'universal (*) and bare attribute selectors in hot rules - no fast-path bucketing by class.' Style engines normally index rules by the rightmost simple selector so an element only considers rules that could match it. A rule whose subject is an attribute rather than a class defeats that index. selector-descendant-vs-flat already showed descendant chains cost a flat 10% in cohtml; this asks whether losing the class bucket costs more than lengthening the chain.
result: CONFIRMED, and the largest selector effect measured: Styles 2.41x / 2.65x / 2.82x, growing slowly with element count. Losing the class bucket costs far more than lengthening a descendant chain - selector-descendant-vs-flat measured a flat 1.10x for two extra ancestors, so an attribute-subject rule is roughly 2.5x worse than a class-subject one. This is the selector finding with real weight behind it, and unlike the descendant-chain result it is large enough to justify tooling or a lint rule.
notes: Applicability gate: DIRECT. The universal selector and attribute selectors are both listed as supported in the feature inventory. Rule 1: one variable, the selector form of the 200 rules. Every rule body is byte-identical between variants and the colours come from the same generator function, so both render the same pixels. Rule 2: identical DOM and identical element count; B additionally sets a data-k attribute, which is what its rules key on - the attribute is the mechanism the variable requires, not an extra element. Rule 3: identical JS apart from that attribute write. Rule 4: no text, no assets. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the class churn IS the case and replaces the shared damage driver; every tile gains or loses .hot every frame, forcing a re-match against the full rule set. Rule 7: no randomness - colours and classes derive from the index. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300 elements against a rule count fixed at 200. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS - the rules are literal CSS because runtime CSS-in-JS is prohibited in Gameface. Rule 10: expected axis is Styles. DIFF SIZE EXCEPTION: like selector-descendant-vs-flat, the diff is the whole rule block because the rule block IS the variable. It stays reviewable because the change is uniform - every selector swaps '.kN' for '* [data-k="N"]' and nothing else differs. Generated by tools/make-rule-heavy-cases.js.
